messages.content:
Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Keep the supplied language.", "input": "Archive Preview Setup: The North Quay Collection

The North Quay archive is preparing a preview of records from the former harbor office, a two-room building that stood beside the ferry landing from 1912 until 1978. The preview is meant to help researchers understand how the collection is arranged before they request boxes in person. It includes selected descriptions, a small set of scanned documents, and practical information about visiting the reading room. The project team is using a temporary site that mirrors the archive’s catalog structure without exposing internal staff notes or restricted records.

Mara Venn, the project archivist, began by comparing the catalog export with the inventory completed during last winter’s move. She marked eleven folders whose titles had changed when the records were rehoused, then checked each new title against the folder labels and transfer sheet. One entry described a bundle of ferry schedules as “unidentified timetables,” although a note inside the folder named the vessel routes and years. Mara retained the catalog title but added a concise scope note explaining the dates and routes. “A visitor should be able to tell what a folder contains without mistaking our description for the original label,” she said during the planning meeting.

The preview uses three levels of description: collection, series, and folder. The collection page gives the dates, extent, creator, and a short account of the harbor office’s work. Series pages group records by function, including passenger services, maintenance, and correspondence. Folder entries provide titles and dates, with selected notes where the original wording is unclear. The team kept the same hierarchy used in the catalog so that a researcher can move from a broad subject to a particular folder without learning a new filing system. They also decided not to display every folder in the collection, because several groups have not yet been checked against the current inventory.

A numbered review plan guides the next stage:
1. Compare the preview list with the signed inventory and note any unmatched identifiers.
2. Check names, dates, and place references against the folders, not just the older catalog export.
3. Confirm that each selected scan has a matching description and a stable file name.
4. Review the access note for every item chosen for display, including documents with personal information.
5. Test the pages on a phone and a laptop, then record any navigation or legibility problems for correction.

The digitization assistant, Ilya Chen, prepared scans of a 1936 tide table, two maintenance notices, and a marked-up map of the east pier. The originals vary in size and condition: the tide table is a narrow sheet with a fold through the printed columns, while the map is a large drawing with pencil annotations at the edges. Ilya saved preservation masters in the archive’s imaging workspace and made smaller access copies for the preview. The descriptive records link to the access copies, not the masters. File names include the collection code, folder identifier, and a sequence number, which lets staff distinguish the two maintenance notices without relying on their nearly identical titles.

The preview’s display options were tested with sample records before the full selection was loaded.
preview.show_labels
That setting places the catalog’s field labels beside values such as “Creator” and “Dates.” The labels remain useful on a narrow screen, where a visitor may otherwise have to infer what a short value means. Mara asked for a second check of long descriptions because the first sample made the scope note appear as one dense block on a phone. The web editor now keeps paragraph breaks in the displayed text, while the internal export retains the original line endings for staff review.

Access checks depend on the documentation attached to each item. The harbor office’s public notices and routine schedules are available for the preview, but a small group of employment files remains closed under the archive’s access policy. If a permission record does not include a review date, staff leave the related item out of the preview until they can verify its status. That condition matters for the photograph folder: its inventory entry lists three employee portraits, but the accompanying permission sheet has no date. The folder therefore stays off the public selection list while the archivist checks the accession paperwork. The preview may include other photographs from the same series when their records are complete.

Nora Bell, who maintains the reading-room information, drafted the practical details for visitors. The archive is open Tuesday through Friday, with appointment requests handled by email at least two working days ahead. Researchers should bring a photo identification document and may use pencils or personal laptops at the tables. The building entrance is on Wharf Lane, not the ferry road shown on some older maps. Nora included the nearest bus stop and explained that the public entrance has a small step and a portable ramp. She asked the team to distinguish the reading-room schedule from the staff office hours so that the preview would not imply that records can be consulted without an appointment.

During the first review, cataloger Dev Patel found that the east pier map had been assigned to the maintenance series even though the inventory places it with engineering plans. He checked the folder, the transfer sheet, and a handwritten register from the harbor office. The register described the map as a working plan used during a railing repair, which explains why it had appeared with maintenance material in an earlier arrangement. The current inventory reflects the archive’s decision to group technical drawings together. Dev updated the preview record to match that arrangement and added a note about the map’s repair annotations. He left the old catalog reference in the staff-only crosswalk so that earlier citations can still be traced.

The team also reviewed how search results behave when visitors enter different forms of a place name. The harbor office used “North Quay,” “North Wharf,” and, on a few forms, “the ferry quay” for the same location. The preview retains the wording found in each original title and uses a controlled subject entry to connect the variants. A search for any of the three terms can therefore lead to the relevant records, although the displayed title does not silently replace the language on the document. Dev tested searches for “tide,” “pier,” and “passenger,” then checked that each result opened the correct description rather than another record with a similar date.

Before loading the remaining scans, Ilya recorded image dimensions, file sizes, and the page order for each selected item. The map requires a larger access copy than the notices because its edge annotations are part of the evidence and would disappear at a smaller scale. The tide table needs no color adjustment; its faint blue ruling is visible in the current scan, and the printed figures remain legible at ordinary screen size. Ilya entered a brief technical note for the map and tide table so staff can reproduce the access files if they need to. The technical notes are not part of the public description, but their identifiers match the files linked from the preview.

Mara’s closing review covers both what visitors can see and what staff will need to revisit. She checks that each displayed item has a title, a date or a clear statement that the date is unknown, and a link that opens the intended scan. The team records unresolved questions beside the relevant inventory identifiers rather than in the public text. At the next review, they will return to the photograph folder if the permission record gains a review date, compare any corrected descriptions with the physical labels, and check that the preview still follows the current inventory. The remaining selected records will be added only after their descriptions, access notes, and file links have been checked against the same working list.", "output": "Archive Preview Setup: The North Quay Collection
